prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This morning I was walking upstairs from the kitchen, carrying your beautiful flowers, the flowers you brought me last night, calla lilies and something else, I am not sure what to call them, white flowers, of course you had no way of knowing it has been years since I bought white flowers—but now you have and here they are again. I was carrying your flowers and a coffee cup and a soft yellow handbag and a book of poems by a Chinese poet, in which I had just read the words “come or go but don’t just stand there in the doorway,” as usual I was carrying too many things, you would have laughed if you saw me. It seemed especially important not to spill the coffee as I usually do, as I turned up the stairs, inside the whorl of the house as if I were walking up inside the lilies. I do not know how to hold all the beauty and sorrow of my life.

outputs.L1:
This morning, I was walking upstairs from the kitchen, carrying your beautiful flowers—the ones you brought me last night: calla lilies and something else, though I am not sure what to call them. White flowers. Of course, you had no way of knowing it has been years since I bought white flowers, but now you have, and here they are again.

I was carrying your flowers, a coffee cup, a soft yellow handbag, and a book of poems by a Chinese poet, in which I had just read the words: “Come or go, but don’t just stand there in the doorway.” As usual, I was carrying too many things; you would have laughed if you had seen me. It seemed especially important not to spill the coffee, as I usually do, as I turned up the stairs, into the whorl of the house, as though I were walking up inside the lilies.

I do not know how to hold all the beauty and sorrow of my life.
outputs.L2: This morning, I was coming up the stairs from the kitchen with the lovely flowers you had given me last night in my arms—calla lilies, and some other white blossoms whose name I don’t know. Naturally, you couldn’t have realized that I had not bought white flowers in years, but now you have brought them, and they are here once more. Along with the flowers, I was holding a cup of coffee, a pale yellow soft handbag, and a book of poems by a Chinese writer. I had just read a line in it that said, “come or go but don’t just stand there in the doorway.” As always, I had taken on more than I could easily carry; if you had been there, you would have laughed at me. While I turned onto the staircase, winding upward through the center of the house as though climbing inside the lilies themselves, it felt unusually necessary not to slosh the coffee the way I usually do. I have no idea how to carry all the grief and beauty that belong to my life.
outputs.L3:
The speaker remembers carrying the flowers that had been given to them the night before: calla lilies and other white blossoms gathered together in their arms. The flowers are striking, not only because of their beauty, but because of what they bring back. White flowers have a particular significance for the speaker, who realizes they have not bought them in years. Their presence stirs a memory that feels both immediate and distant, as though the flowers have opened a door to something long avoided or forgotten.

At the same time, the speaker is physically overloaded. They are trying to manage too many things at once: the bouquet, a cup of coffee, a handbag, and a book of poems. The objects become more than ordinary belongings; they seem to mirror the speaker’s emotional state. Everything is beautiful, meaningful, and cumbersome all at once.

A line from the poetry book rises into the moment: “come or go but don’t just stand there in the doorway.” The phrase resonates deeply, capturing a feeling of being suspended between movement and stillness, arrival and departure, memory and the present. Like the speaker, the line seems to demand a decision, or at least an end to hesitation.

In this moment, the speaker is overcome by the strange coexistence of beauty and sorrow. The flowers are lovely, the poem is powerful, and yet both carry an ache. Life appears crowded with objects, memories, and emotions that cannot be easily separated. The speaker is left holding all of it at once: the tenderness of beauty, the weight of grief, and the difficulty of moving forward.
outputs.L4:
In the morning I tried to carry too much.

It was not the first time. I had come in from the market with a paper-wrapped bunch of flowers pressed against my chest, a cup of coffee balanced carefully in one hand, my handbag slipping from the bend of my elbow, and a book of poems tucked under my arm. The stairs rose in front of me, ordinary and familiar, each step catching the pale light from the window above. Nothing dramatic was happening. No one would have stopped to notice me. I was only going upstairs.

And yet, halfway up, I felt the whole arrangement begin to tremble.

The coffee leaned dangerously toward its lid. The flowers rustled against my coat, their stems damp and cold through the paper. My bag pulled downward, heavy with keys, receipts, a phone, a wallet, the small debris of being alive. The book of poems, which I had bought without planning to, pressed into my ribs as if insisting on its own presence. I paused there on the stairs, one foot lifted, one hand full, my body trying to solve the small problem of balance.

That was when I thought: this is what it is like to live.

Not in the grand moments, not only in grief or celebration, but in this ridiculous and tender effort to hold everything at once. Flowers and coffee. Errands and beauty. Language and appetite. The need to get upstairs and the sudden awareness that every simple movement is crowded with feeling.

The flowers were for the table, though I knew they would not last. Already one petal had loosened and fallen against my sleeve. The coffee was growing cooler. The handbag contained things I needed and things I had forgotten were there. The book of poems reminded me of someone I loved, someone who used to read aloud in the kitchen, making even silence afterward feel inhabited.

I stood there and thought of how much we are asked to carry: the sweetness of a morning, the ache of what is gone, the faces of the living, the voices of the dead, the errands, the bills, the weather, the sudden beauty of flowers in brown paper, the private catastrophes no one sees. All the beauty and sorrow of it. All of it gathered into the arms at once.

For a moment, I nearly dropped everything.

But I did not. I shifted the book more securely under my arm, tightened my hold on the flowers, lifted the coffee again, and climbed the rest of the stairs slowly. Each step required attention. Each step was a small act of faith.

By the time I reached the top, nothing had changed. The morning was still the morning. The flowers still needed water. The coffee was still warm enough to drink. The poems were still waiting to be opened.

But I had been changed, if only slightly, by the knowledge that ordinary life is never merely ordinary. It is always carrying more than it appears to carry. A person on the stairs with her hands full may be holding breakfast, blossoms, a bag, a book. She may also be holding memory, love, loss, and the impossible weight of being here.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, introspective prose poem in first person about carrying flowers, coffee, a handbag, and a poetry book upstairs, ending with a meditation on beauty and sorrow.
counterfactuals.output:
I carry the flowers first, because they are the most alive, their stems knocking softly against the paper, their heads leaning together as if sharing a secret about rain. Under one arm I tuck the poetry book, its pages already loosening from use, already holding the fingerprints of other evenings. In my hand, the coffee cools in its paper cup, a small dark moon I am careful not to spill. My handbag hangs from my elbow, heavy with the ordinary evidence of being here: keys, receipts, a pen that does not write, a mirror clouded at the edges.

On the stairs I become a procession of my own burdens. Each step asks me to arrange myself again. The flowers brush the wall. The coffee trembles. The book slides, then steadies. I feel, absurdly, like a person in a painting meant to represent morning, or devotion, or the difficult grace of returning home. No one sees me pause on the landing to catch my breath, but still I lift my face as though watched by some benevolent witness, some tender god of thresholds and stairwells.

I think of all the things we carry upward without knowing whether they will last: warmth in a cup, fragrance in a room, language against silence, a body through another day. The flowers are already leaving themselves. The coffee is already losing heat. The poems were written by people who could not remain, yet here they are, climbing with me, close to my ribs.

At the door, I shift everything to find my keys, and for a moment the whole fragile arrangement threatens to fall. This, too, is a kind of prayer: to keep hold, to enter, to set beauty down before it vanishes. And perhaps sorrow is not the opposite of beauty, but the shadow that lets it be seen—the dark stair beneath the bright bouquet, the bitter coffee beside the singing page, the ache in my arm that tells me I have carried something precious this far.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph in the style of contemporary literary fiction: someone receives white flowers from a lover, walks up from the kitchen with too many things, and is overwhelmed by memory and feeling.
counterfactuals.output: The flowers were waiting in the sink when she came in, white lilies wrapped in damp paper, their throats pale and expectant, as if they had been interrupted mid-breath. She read his name on the card and then stood there too long, one hand still on the refrigerator door, the cold light spilling over her shoes. By the time she started upstairs she was carrying everything badly: the flowers in the crook of her arm, a glass of water pressed between two fingers, her phone, the mail, the little knife she had used to cut the string. Halfway up, the lilies knocked against the wall and released their heavy sweetness, and suddenly she was not in the house but in every room they had ever left behind—the hotel with the cracked basin, his winter coat on her chair, the morning he said nothing and touched her hair as though memorizing a language he would soon forget. The water tipped over her wrist, ran down into her sleeve, and she stopped on the stairs, absurdly burdened, pierced by the tenderness of being remembered and the terror of what memory chose to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic monologue addressed to “you” that includes calla lilies, a coffee cup, a yellow handbag, a Chinese poet’s line about a doorway, and the sentence “I do not know how to hold all the beauty and sorrow of my life.”
counterfactuals.output:
You stand there as if the morning has chosen you  
from all its small astonishments—  
the coffee cup warm between your hands,  
the yellow handbag bright as a little sun  
set down beside the chair.

Calla lilies lean from the vase,  
white throats open to the room,  
each one a silence shaped like listening.  
I want to tell you how they remind me  
of all the things we could not say  
without breaking.

Somewhere in my notebook  
I have written a Chinese poet’s line:  
“Beyond the doorway, the spring wind keeps calling.”  
And I think of you at every threshold—  
arriving, departing,  
turning back once,  
as if love were a house  
you had almost remembered how to enter.

You ask me what I am afraid of,  
and I look at the lilies,  
the cup, the yellow handbag,  
the doorway full of light,  
and I say nothing at first.

Then I say:  
“I do not know how to hold all the beauty and sorrow of my life.”

But you, you keep standing there,  
and the morning keeps pouring itself  
over your shoulders,  
and even grief, for a moment,  
looks almost tender.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tender, melancholic scene where the narrator carries flowers given the night before and thinks about grief, love, and the difficulty of holding everything at once.
counterfactuals.output:
By morning, the flowers had begun to bow.

Only slightly—the way a person lowers their head to listen more closely, or to hide that they are crying. Their stems were still firm in my hand, wrapped in brown paper darkened where my palm had sweated through it, and the ribbon from the night before trailed loose against my wrist. I had not cut the ends. I had not put them in water. I had carried them home as if carrying them were enough to keep them alive.

You had given them to me beneath the yellow light outside the restaurant, after the rain had stopped and the pavement held the whole city upside down in its shallow black mirrors. There had been lilies, blue irises, a few pale roses with petals soft as breath. I remembered your face as you offered them—half hopeful, half shy, though we are long past the age of shyness. I remembered thinking: how strange, to be handed beauty when I was already so full of ache.

Now I walked with them through the park, the morning cold touching my cheeks, the sky the flat grey of old pewter. The paths were slick with fallen leaves. A dog barked somewhere and was answered by another, farther away. Ordinary sounds. Ordinary life continuing in its stubborn, almost offensive way.

I thought of my mother then, because grief comes to me like weather—unannounced, familiar, arriving over whatever landscape I happen to be standing in. She would have loved these flowers. She would have taken them from me briskly, scolding me for not putting them in water, trimming their stems at an angle with the good kitchen knife. She would have chosen a vase without appearing to think about it. She would have known how to make them last.

That was one of the cruelest things about her absence: all the small, precise knowledges that had vanished with her. How much salt. Which drawer. When to turn the heat down. How to bear a life without making it seem like bearing.

I held the bouquet closer.

Last night, when you kissed me, I had wanted to cry—not from unhappiness, not exactly, but from the impossible tenderness of being loved while still belonging so deeply to loss. There are moments when love does not rescue you from grief so much as sit beside it, awkward and warm, unsure where to put its hands. Your fingers had brushed mine around the paper, and I had felt both grateful and terrified. Grateful because you were there. Terrified because presence is always the first shape of future absence.

The flowers rustled in my arms. A petal loosened and fell, landing on the wet path like a small surrendered flag.

I stopped walking.

For a while I simply stood there, holding what had been given to me. The bouquet was not heavy, but it felt like everything: your kindness, my mother’s hands, the years behind me, the years I was afraid to want. I thought about how the heart is asked to be a room large enough for all of it—the dead and the living, longing and memory, joy with its bright face pressed against sorrow’s darkened window.

No one teaches you how to hold them at once. You learn by failing. You crush some things. You drop others. You grip too tightly, then not tightly enough. You walk through the morning with yesterday’s flowers, ashamed of their wilting, unable to let them go.

The wind moved gently through the bare trees. I bent and picked up the fallen petal, though there was no reason to save it. It rested in my palm, bruised at the edge, still faintly fragrant.

Then I went on, slowly, toward home—toward water, a vase, the small necessary rituals by which we pretend we can keep anything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness prose piece with long flowing sentences, domestic details, white flowers, stairs, spilled coffee, and an emotional realization at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
In the morning, before the house had decided what mood to wear, I stood in the kitchen with one hand on the counter and the other wrapped around a cup of coffee gone too hot at the rim and too bitter at the center, watching the steam rise and loosen itself into the pale light, while the sink held its small evidence of last night’s surrender—a spoon with a crescent of yogurt dried along its bowl, two plates leaned together like conspirators, a knife striped with butter, and the green glass vase on the windowsill, the one with the hairline crack I kept meaning to replace, held three white flowers I had bought at the corner shop because they looked calm, because they looked as if nothing had ever been asked of them, because I wanted something in the room that did not remember.

The house creaked around me in its old familiar grammar, heat ticking in the pipes, the refrigerator humming like someone refusing to answer, a car passing outside with tires whispering over damp pavement, and I thought of laundry in the basket at the foot of the stairs, how the sleeves had knotted themselves together, how one sock had dropped onto the landing yesterday and remained there all night, small and dark and accusing, while upstairs the unmade bed kept the shape of two people who had slept without touching, or had tried to sleep, or had lain awake listening to each other breathe with the care of enemies not wanting to wake the war.

I don’t know why I turned so quickly, perhaps because the kettle clicked off or because a bird hit the gutter with a sharp metallic scramble or because I heard, impossibly, your voice saying my name from the hall, but my elbow knocked the cup and the coffee went over the counter in a brown, glossy rush, spreading toward the bills, the school photograph magneted crookedly to the fridge, the edge of the recipe card in my mother’s handwriting, and then down the cabinet face in slow vertical lines like varnish or rain or something a house might weep if given permission, and I stood there, ridiculous and still, watching it drip onto the floorboards instead of reaching for a towel.

The white flowers did not move, though one petal had fallen onto the sill, and beyond them the day brightened with that indifferent kindness mornings have, filling the kitchen, touching the spilled coffee, the chair with your sweater on it, the stairs rising from the hallway in their narrow turn, each step crowded with ordinary tasks—carry up the towels, bring down the glasses, find the library book, change the bulb, say the thing, don’t say the thing—and suddenly I could see myself climbing them last night behind you, my hand hovering over the banister, wanting to call you back but stopping at the same step where the sock lay, as if the whole house had been arranged to show me the exact height at which pride becomes loneliness.

And there, with coffee cooling around my bare feet and the smell of it dark and earthy and final, with the white flowers opening their clean faces to the window and the stairs waiting in the hall like a question I had postponed for years, I understood not that you had left, or that you might leave, or that love had thinned beyond repair, but something quieter and more terrible: I had mistaken being unhurt for being safe, and in doing so had made a home where even tenderness had to knock before entering.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
